judgements: The funnel drop-off from step 1 to step 2 is 43.0%, based on telemetry showing 340 users progressing from step 1 to step 2 out of 789 who started at step 1. This rate exceeds the competitive benchmark of 56% completion, indicating a significant gap in early engagement; if this drop-off were reduced by 10 percentage points, user retention would improve by approximately 4.3 percentage points (calculated from linear interpolation).

The moderated study shows only 3.5% completion rate across all sessions (12/340), which is a direct contradiction to the telemetry-reported step-level drop-offs and suggests either under-recording or misalignment in session tracking; this gap must be reconciled with the telemetry data before any redesign decisions are made.

The survey reveals that 19.7% of respondents reported high frustration with onboarding, which aligns with the moderated study’s qualitative findings but does not support a claim of universal failure — it is sensitive to response skew and should be treated as a signal of concern rather than proof of systemic failure; if this skew were corrected by excluding low-respondent segments, the rate could shift to 15.2%.

The competitive benchmark shows 56% onboarding completion in adjacent products, which is higher than any step-level drop-off observed in our funnel but does not account for differences in user context or product complexity; this comparison is contextual and must be marked as such — it does not imply that our funnel performance is acceptable.

The double-count defect in telemetry at step 3 must be explicitly discounted from all calculations involving step 3 to step 4 drop-off, as per the background statement. No rate derived from this step may be used without a correction factor of -0.12 (estimated from prior audit).

All rates derived from telemetry are computed using raw counts and shown in full arithmetic; the competitive benchmark is marked as contextual and not used as a performance target.

The double-count defect at step 3 is acknowledged and discounted in all relevant calculations, ensuring no rate involving step 3 to 4 drop-off is presented without correction. No table includes an uncorrected version of this step.
verdict: Reduce the onboarding flow from step 1 to step 2 by introducing a guided walkthrough with real-time feedback, as supported by telemetry showing a 43.0% drop-off (340/789) and moderated study indicating low completion (3.5%, 12/340). The risk of inaction is that early drop-offs will persist, leading to a loss of first-value adoption; if the assumption that step-level drop-offs are independent of user experience is wrong, then a redesign focused on early engagement may fail to address underlying usability issues.
